Grete died in the night of the twelfth to the thirteenth of November two thousand and thirty-six, in her room at the care home, room fourteen, in her sleep, without pain, as the doctor said in the morning, “as peacefully as you could wish”. She was a hundred years and six months old. It had been a Wednesday. In the evening Elif had played for her, as she had almost every evening since the letter to Mrs Petersen, on the freshly tuned piano in the common room, with the door open. She had played the little Chopin waltz and the Brahms Intermezzo, and then, as an encore, because Mara, who was sitting by Grete's bed, had asked her to, a children's song Grete had taught her three years before, right at the start, when Elif didn't yet know where C was on the keyboard. “Weißt du, wie viel Sternlein stehen” (Do you know how many little stars there are). Grete didn't open her eyes. But she smiled. That's what Mara said later. She smiled, at the last verse.

Mrs Petersen rang Ludwig at half past six. Ludwig was already awake. He was sitting in the kitchen, with a cup of coffee that had gone cold, and when the phone rang, he knew before he answered. He only said: “Thank you for calling me”, and then he stood there for a long time, with the receiver in his hand, and looked out of the window into the courtyard, at the chestnut tree, which was losing its last yellow leaves, one after another, slowly, without any wind. Then he got up, put on his grey coat and his tram driver's cap and went out, to the brass bell in the café, which was still closed, unlocked it with his key, lifted the felt, although it wasn't nine yet, and rang. Twice. Very quietly. With his finger, not with the cord. Dr Vogt, who was just coming back from his night shift, heard it on the stairs and stopped.

Hotte was the last to find out, because he had no phone and only came into the café around midday, although it wasn't Thursday. He saw it on their faces before anyone said anything. He didn't sit down. He went through the café, through the back door, into the courtyard, to the chestnut tree, and stood there, leaning on his two walking sticks, with his back to the window, for a long time. Nobody went to him. Lena wanted to, but Ludwig held her by the arm. “Leave him”, he said quietly. “He's known her since nineteen seventy. Longer than I have.” When Hotte finally came back, his cap was in his hand and not on his head, for the first time anyone could remember. He sat down at his table, ordered a coffee and said a single sentence, to nobody: “She slapped me in nineteen seventy-two. I deserved it. I never thanked her.”

In the afternoon Mrs Petersen read the letter. Grete had written it in July, or rather dictated it, to Elif, who at the time hadn't known what it was for, because Grete had told her it was “an exercise in bureaucratic German”. Elif recognised her own handwriting when Mrs Petersen opened the envelope, and went pale. Mara took her hand. It was a short letter, one page, in a German that was at once formal and entirely Grete. She didn't want a sad service, it said. Nobody was to wear black, “except Hotte, nothing else suits him”. There was to be music, and played by children, “not by professionals, they've had enough applause already”. And there was to be cake, from Lena, “but not the one with raisins, I could never stand that one, I just never told her”.

Then came the belongings. Her sheet music, all eight hundred and twelve pieces, which she had collected over seventy years and, as she wrote, “counted on a boring night in the year two thousand and twenty-nine”, was to be handed over to Elif, “with the request that she not play all of it, only the good ones”. Her black hat with the feather was to go to Lena, “for the next wedding, which is sure to come, I know it, she doesn't know it yet”. Lena, who was sitting next to Ludwig, laughed through her tears. The metronome she had already given to Elif. Her savings, a sum that surprised none of those who knew how frugally Grete had lived, were to go to the scholarship that bore Friedrich's name, on one single condition: that from now on it be called the “Friedrich and Margarete Scholarship”. “He's been alone on the plaque long enough”, she had dictated. “Now I'm coming too.”

The sheet music arrived two days later, in three removal boxes, which Andrei and Leo carried into the Yilmaz family's flat, on the second floor of number thirty-three. Elif opened them alone, in her room, in the evening, and leafed through them until midnight. On almost every page there was something in the margin, in pencil, in Grete's small, slanting handwriting, from seventy different years: “Don't rush!” “Breathe here.” “Left hand quieter, it's not the main character.” “For F., 1961.” “Too hard for me. For now.” And on the last sheet of a Bach prelude, right at the bottom, in handwriting that already trembled, so from the last years: “For the child who comes after me. She will play better than me. That is the point of it all.” Elif read the sentence three times. Then she put the sheet under her pillow and slept, for the first time since the thirteenth of November, a whole night, without dreams, until morning.

Right at the end came the matter of the ashes. Half were to be scattered at Travemünde, on the Baltic, at the same spot where Friedrich's ashes had been scattered in May two thousand and thirty-four, “so that we don't lose each other”. The other half, and here Mrs Petersen paused, because her voice was no longer quite steady, was to be buried under the chestnut tree in the courtyard at Kastanienallee thirty-one, “if the owner of the house has no objection, and if he has any objection, he should be reminded who taught him to waltz in nineteen eighty-two”. Ludwig laughed, for the first time that day, and at the same time tears ran down his face. He had forgotten. The waltz. At Ingrid's sister's wedding. He had trodden on Grete's feet, three times, and she had said he danced like a tram driver. Forty-four years before she said the same thing about how he played the guitar.

The memorial service was on Saturday, the twenty-second of November, at three in the afternoon, in the large hall of the care home, where Grete had celebrated her hundredth birthday. Nobody wore black, except Hotte, who came in a black suit which, as he said, he had “borrowed specially for Grete” and which was two sizes too big for him. Everyone else wore colours. Elif wore a red dress that Ayşe had sewn for her, in the colour of Grete's lipstick. Lena wore the black hat with the feather, the only black item on her, and, as she whispered to Ludwig, “only because that was her wish”. And on the cake table there wasn't a single raisin cake. Lena, the evening before, when she had read that, had laughed out loud, then cried, then baked a poppy-seed cake.

Elena was there too. She should actually have gone back to Sibiu on Monday, the ten weeks were over, but she had changed her ticket without thinking twice. She wore a dark green dress with embroidery at the collar, which she had sewn herself, and sat in the third row, next to Yusuf, whom she had invited and who had come, even though he had never met Grete. “She gave me a sentence for my mother”, he told Ludwig, when asked why he had come. “Not every note. The melody. My mother wrote it on a slip of paper and stuck it on her fridge in Aleppo. I can't stay at home after something like that.”

Only children played, as Grete had wished. Elif played, of course. But not only her. Eleven children came, all between seven and fifteen, all pupils Grete had taught in the last three years, on Wednesdays, at the care home, or whose parents Grete had taught thirty or forty years before, when she still lived on Kastanienallee. Each child played a single piece, the shortest they knew, some with mistakes, some too fast, a little boy of seven played only a scale, C major, up and down, and bowed so deeply afterwards that he almost fell off the stage. Nobody laughed at him. Everyone clapped. And Hotte, in his oversized black suit, clapped loudest and shouted: “Bravo! Grete would've loved that! She started with a scale too!”

Elif played last. She didn't play the Intermezzo. She had thought for a long time about what to play, and in the end, among the eight hundred and twelve pieces of sheet music she had received two days before in three removal boxes, she had found something she hadn't expected: a single yellowed sheet, handwritten, in handwriting that wasn't Grete's, but older, finer, in an almost faded pencil. At the top it said: “For M. H., to practise on the table. W., 1946.” It was a small piece, sixteen bars, very simple, for beginners. Mr Wendland had written it for her, for the girl who played on the kitchen table. Elif played it twice. Once on the piano. And once, at the end, without sound, on the lid of the piano, with her eyes closed, the way Grete had played it in nineteen forty-six on the kitchen table. And the hall was so quiet that you could hear the clock ticking on the wall.

In December, shortly before Christmas, Ludwig, Mara, Jakob and Elif took the train to Lübeck and from there the bus to Travemünde, with a small urn in Mara's bag. It was cold and windy, and the Baltic was grey, with white crests of foam, and there was nobody on the beach except them and an old man with a dog. They went to the spot where they had scattered Friedrich's ashes in May two thousand and thirty-four, by the third groyne behind the old lighthouse, and Mara opened the urn, and the wind took the ashes, faster than they had thought, and carried them over the water, to the east, where Friedrich's ashes had been carried two and a half years before. Nobody said anything. Then Elif hummed, very quietly, against the wind, Mr Wendland's sixteen bars. The old man with the dog stopped and listened until she had finished, nodded and walked on, without asking.

In spring, on a Saturday in April, when the chestnut tree in the courtyard had its first leaves, the second half of Grete's ashes was buried under the tree, in a small urn of light-coloured wood that Andrei had made, with a single bird carved on the lid, the fifty-fourth. Ludwig had no objection. Of course not. Next to it, in the ground, Elif stuck a little sign she had painted herself, on a piece of wood, in her round, neat handwriting: “Grete lives here. Please ring.” And from then on, when someone came into the café «Bei Ingrid» and pulled the cord of the brass bell, Elif would sometimes glance briefly out of the window into the courtyard, at the chestnut tree. Only very briefly. And then she played on, on an old piano from the care home's second common room, which Mrs Petersen had given to the café, at Grete's wish, “so that the guests have something to listen to, apart from Hotte”.

Margarete Hoffmann, pianist and piano teacher, fell asleep peacefully in the night to 13 November, at the age of a hundred.
She is said to have taught more than a thousand children in seventy years. Her memoirs, “The Girl at the Table”, were published this year.
In her last letter she wrote that nobody was to wear black. There was to be music, played by children.
Without her, much less piano would have been played in Pankow. Those who knew her are glad to have known her.
